diseases.name: Foot and Mouth Disease (FMD)
diseases.clinical_signs: Blisters/vesicles on tongue, lips, gums, and between hooves. Stringy, ropy salivation hanging from mouth. Severe limping/lameness. High fever (104-106°F) and sudden drop in milk production.
first_aid: Isolate affected animals immediately in a clean, shaded enclosure to prevent herd transmission.
Wash mouth lesions gently with 1% potassium permanganate (KMnO4) or mild alum water.
Apply a soothing paste of boric acid and glycerin on oral ulcers.
Clean foot lesions with copper sulphate solution (2%) or antiseptic, and apply neem/turpentine oil to prevent fly maggots.
Feed soft, palatable gruel (boiled rice/maize daliya with jaggery) since animal cannot chew coarse fodder.
preventive_measures: Bi-annual vaccination under the National Animal Disease Control Programme (NADCP).
Quarantine any newly purchased cattle or buffalo for at least 21 days.
Disinfect farm perimeter, vehicles, and equipment with 4% sodium carbonate.
diseases.disclaimer: FMD is highly contagious. Prompt reporting to the nearest Veterinary Dispensary is mandatory.

diseases.name: Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD)
diseases.clinical_signs: Firm round nodules (2-5 cm) erupting across skin of head, neck, body, udder, and limbs. High fever (104-106°F), enlarged prescapular lymph nodes, edema of legs/brisket, and watery nasal/ocular discharge.
first_aid: Quarantine the affected animal immediately in a mosquito/fly-proof shed.
Spray cattle sheds with natural mosquito/tick repellents or light neem leaf smoke at dusk.
Clean burst skin nodules with 1% povidone-iodine and apply turmeric-neem paste to repel flies and prevent secondary bacterial infection.
Provide continuous fresh water enriched with oral rehydration salts and electrolytes.
preventive_measures: Immunize with Goat Pox vaccine (heterologous) or Lumpi-ProVacInd vaccine as guided by state veterinary department.
Intensive vector control (spraying against biting flies, mosquitoes, and ticks).
Restrict movement of livestock from affected areas.
diseases.disclaimer: LSD weakens cattle and can lead to secondary infections. Consult a registered veterinarian for fever management and supportive therapy.

diseases.name: Bovine Mastitis
diseases.clinical_signs: Swollen, hard, hot, or visibly painful udder/quarter. Milk contains clots, flakes, blood, or appears watery/yellowish. The animal kicks or resists milking due to intense discomfort.
first_aid: Perform complete, gentle stripping of milk from the affected quarter every 2-3 hours and safely discard the milk.
Apply cold water compresses or ice packs if the udder is acutely hot, inflamed, and swollen.
Perform teat dipping in 0.5% povidone-iodine solution after each milking session.
Always milk healthy cows first and the affected animal last to prevent cross-contamination.
Keep the cow standing for 30 minutes after milking by offering feed, allowing teat sphincters to close.
preventive_measures: Ensure dry, clean bedding (sand or clean dry straw) in cattle resting areas.
Perform periodic California Mastitis Test (CMT) screening for subclinical detection.
Implement dry cow antibiotic therapy under veterinary direction before drying off.
diseases.disclaimer: Untreated mastitis causes permanent fibrosis and quarter loss. Professional veterinary intramammary infusion and antibiotic sensitivity testing are essential.

diseases.name: Hemorrhagic Septicemia (HS)
diseases.clinical_signs: Sudden onset of very high fever (106-107°F). Hot, painful, tense inflammatory swelling in throat, submandibular space, and dewlap. Rapid shallow breathing with loud snoring/grunting sounds, tongue protruding, and severe respiratory distress.
first_aid: IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY: Contact a veterinarian or dial 1962 emergency mobile unit without delay.
Do NOT tie tight ropes around the neck or dewlap; keep the animal's neck extended to assist airflow.
Isolate from all other livestock immediately in a cool, well-ventilated space.
Keep the animal strictly stationary; avoid any physical exertion or stress.
preventive_measures: Annual pre-monsoon vaccination (May-June) before monsoon humidity peaks.
Maintain high hygiene during weather transitions and avoid mixing with migrating herds.
diseases.disclaimer: CRITICAL EMERGENCY: HS progresses rapidly and can be fatal within 12-24 hours without immediate veterinary antibiotic injections.

diseases.name: Black Quarter (BQ)
diseases.clinical_signs: Acute severe lameness in young stock (6-24 months). High fever (105-106°F). Hot, painful swelling on heavy muscle masses (thigh, shoulder, neck) that rapidly turns cold, painless, and produces a distinct crackling/crepitation sound when pressed due to gas accumulation.
first_aid: IMMEDIATE EMERGENCY: Call a veterinary doctor immediately.
Do NOT puncture, cut, or massage the muscle swelling, as Clostridium spores will contaminate the pasture soil permanently.
Keep the animal comfortable on soft bedding to prevent pressure sores.
Separate from other young calves immediately.
preventive_measures: Annual pre-monsoon BQ polyvalent vaccination.
Deep burial (with quicklime) or incineration of dead carcasses; never open carcasses in open ground.
diseases.disclaimer: CRITICAL EMERGENCY: BQ is an acute, fatal toxemia requiring immediate veterinary intervention.

diseases.name: Acute Ruminal Tympany (Bloat)
diseases.clinical_signs: Severe, sudden ballooning/distension of the left flank (rumen) that sounds like a drum when tapped. Restlessness, kicking at belly, frequent urination/defecation attempts, labored breathing with neck outstretched, open mouth, and protruding tongue.
first_aid: EMERGENCY: Elevate the animal's front legs on a raised slope/mound to reduce rumen pressure against the lungs and diaphragm.
Fasten a smooth wooden bit or clean thick rope horizontally inside the mouth like a bridle to induce continuous chewing and belching (eructation).
Administer 250-400 ml of edible vegetable oil (mustard or peanut oil) mixed with 30 ml turpentine oil under guidance as an antifoaming agent.
Walk the animal slowly on an incline if it can stand.
In life-threatening asphyxiation where the animal collapses, an experienced veterinarian will perform emergency trocarization of the left flank.
preventive_measures: Never feed wet, dewy, or immature leguminous crops (berseem, lucerne) on an empty stomach.
Feed dry straw or coarse hay before turning animals out to lush green pastures.
diseases.disclaimer: CRITICAL EMERGENCY: Severe bloat compresses the thoracic cavity and can cause suffocation and heart failure within hours if untreated.

diseases.name: Milk Fever (Hypocalcemia)
diseases.clinical_signs: Occurs within 24-72 hours post-calving in high-yield dairy cows. Initial muscle trembling progresses to recumbency (lying down unable to rise). Characteristic 'S-shaped' neck curvature with head resting on flank. Cold ears, horns, and feet. Subnormal body temperature (97-100°F). Dry muzzle and dilated pupils.
first_aid: CRITICAL RULE: NEVER DRENCH MEDICINES OR FLUIDS ORALLY. Swallowing reflexes are paralyzed; fluid will enter the lungs causing fatal aspiration pneumonia.
Prop the cow into sternal recumbency (sitting upright on chest) using straw bales to avoid regurgitation.
Massage ears, neck, and limbs vigorously with dry straw to maintain peripheral circulation.
Call veterinary doctor immediately for intravenous Calcium Borogluconate administration.
preventive_measures: Feed low-calcium, balanced-mineral rations during the late dry period (last 2-3 weeks).
Administer oral calcium gel paste at the time of calving and a second dose 12-24 hours later.
diseases.disclaimer: CRITICAL EMERGENCY: Hypocalcemia is fatal if calcium levels are not restored intravenously by a qualified veterinarian.

diseases.name: Bovine Theileriosis & Tick Fever
diseases.clinical_signs: Persistent high fever (105-107°F). Marked swelling of superficial lymph nodes (in front of shoulder). Severe anemia with pale or yellowish mucous membranes (gums and eyes). In Babesiosis cases, distinct dark red or coffee-colored urine ('Red Water'). Rapid breathing and emaciation.
first_aid: Keep the animal in a shaded, well-ventilated stall on deep bedding.
Provide unlimited cool drinking water with glucose/electrolytes to maintain hydration.
Manually inspect and remove visible ticks around ears, udder, dewlap, and tail base.
Avoid any heavy physical movement or exertion due to severe oxygen-carrying deficits.
preventive_measures: Vaccinate crossbred cattle with Rakshavac-T vaccine as recommended.
Regular application of acaricides (flumethrin/deltamethrin sprays or pour-ons) to control tick vectors.
Burn or crack-seal shed crevices where ticks hide.
diseases.disclaimer: Protozoal blood parasites require specific antiprotozoal drugs (Buparvaquone/Diminazene) administered strictly by a veterinarian.

diseases.name: Bovine Brucellosis
diseases.clinical_signs: Abortion during the 6th to 8th month of pregnancy. Retention of placenta / afterbirth. Persistent foul-smelling vaginal discharge (metritis). Swelling of joints (hygroma) and reduced fertility in herd.
first_aid: CRITICAL ZOONOTIC DANGER: Brucellosis infects humans (causes undulant fever). ALWAYS WEAR GLOVES AND FACE MASK.
Do NOT touch aborted fetus, placenta, or fluid discharge bare-handed.
Immediately burn or deeply bury (at least 6 feet with quicklime) all aborted materials.
Isolate aborted cow for at least 30 days and thoroughly disinfect the calving pen with 2% sodium hydroxide or bleaching powder.
NEVER consume raw, unboiled milk from suspected cattle.
preventive_measures: Mandatory one-time vaccination of female calves aged 4-8 months with Brucella abortus S19 vaccine under NADCP.
Screen all breeding bulls and replacement heifers with serum agglutination tests.
diseases.disclaimer: Brucellosis poses serious public health risks to farmers and consumers. Immediately report abortions to the animal husbandry department.

diseases.name: Bovine Respiratory Disease (Pneumonia)
diseases.vernacular_name: निमोनिया व श्वास रोग (Pneumonia / Shwas Rog)
diseases.clinical_signs: Frequent dry or moist coughing, bilateral nasal discharge (watery progressing to thick mucus/pus), rapid shallow breathing, fever (103-105°F), drooped head and ears, and loss of appetite, especially in young calves during winter or damp seasons.
first_aid: Move the animal into a dry, warm, draft-free shelter with clean bedding.
Provide warm drinking water and soft, easily digestible fodder.
Clean crusted nasal discharge with warm saline water and cotton swabs.
Isolate sick calves from healthy calves to stop aerosol spread.
preventive_measures: Ensure calves receive 3-4 liters of maternal colostrum within the first 2 hours of life.
Maintain adequate ventilation without exposing animals to direct cold nighttime drafts.
Avoid overcrowding and damp bedding in sheds.
diseases.disclaimer: Respiratory infections in cattle can rapidly progress to irreversible lung consolidation. Early veterinary antibiotic intervention is vital.

Head & Mouth.label: Blisters/sores on mouth, tongue or lips
Severe hot swelling in throat/dewlap area
Watery or purulent eye and nasal discharge

Breathing & Lungs.label: Loud snoring, wheezing, or grunting breath sounds

Skin & Legs.label: Multiple firm round lumps/nodules on skin
Sudden acute severe lameness in young animal
Swelling on shoulder/thigh with crackling gas sound

Udder & Milk.label: Swollen, hard, hot, or painful udder
Milk with flakes, clots, or watery color
Blood or yellow pus in milk
Sudden severe drop in milk production

Digestion & Flank.label: Severe drum-like ballooning/swelling of left flank (Bloat)
Restlessness, kicking at belly, colic signs
Complete refusal to eat or chew cud

General & Mobility.label: Animal lying down, unable to rise (Downer cow)
Ears, muzzle and legs feel unusually cold
Neck curved, head resting against flank
Premature abortion in 6th-8th month of pregnancy
